items: You declare desired state; Terraform computes the actions.
Not a script — you never order the steps yourself.
Apply is not a transaction: there is no rollback.
A failed apply leaves partial infrastructure recorded in state.
`terraform plan` never writes managed infrastructure.
Modern versions never persist the refreshed state either.
Output is a proposal, not a promise.
Unknowns can resolve at apply into values the API rejects.

lines: # exact reviewed diff, no yes prompt

items: Bare `terraform apply` plans internally and prompts `yes`.
`-auto-approve` skips that prompt.
The plan file embeds the state snapshot it used.
Serial moved since? `Saved plan is stale` — re-plan.

blocks.title: Never Commit tfplan
blocks.text: A plan file is not encrypted: variable values, resource attributes and secrets sit in it in plaintext.

blocks.q: How do I prove there is no perpetual diff?
a_bullets: The second plan must say `No changes.`
A non-empty second plan is a perpetual-diff bug.

items: Every run builds a fresh directed acyclic graph.
Nodes: resources, data sources, providers, variables, locals.
Outputs and module calls are nodes too.
Edges come from references, never from file order.
Explicit edge for hidden runtime dependencies.
Classic: an IAM policy the instance needs at boot.
Must be a static reference list, never a computed expression.
On a `module` block it applies to every resource inside.

blocks.title: Coarse And Slow
blocks.text: Module-level `depends_on` serializes the walk. Prefer real attribute references wherever one exists.

lines: # mutual refs or a depends_on loop

items: Fix by splitting into `aws_security_group_rule` resources.
Standalone rules break the mutual reference.
`terraform graph` prints DOT; pipe it to Graphviz.
`terraform graph -type=plan` shows the plan-time graph.
Independent nodes run concurrently: default 10.
Tune with `-parallelism=n`.
`create_before_destroy` inverts that pair's edge direction.
New object exists before the old one is removed.

blocks.title: Provider Nodes
items: Dependency of every resource that uses them.
Provider configured from a resource attribute = chicken-and-egg.
Break it with a separate bootstrap root module.

blocks.q: When is a data source node read?
a_bullets: At plan time when its arguments are known.
Deferred to apply when it depends on unknowns.
The graph itself is never persisted — rebuilt every run.

items: Maps config addresses to real object IDs.
Plus the last-known attribute values of each object.
It is the only link between HCL and reality.
Sensitive attributes are stored in plaintext.

blocks.title: Encrypt The Backend
blocks.text: S3 with SSE or Terraform Cloud, and restrict read access the way you would a secret store.

items: Provider `ReadResource` runs per managed resource.
Updates in-memory state before the diff is computed.
Cost is O(number of resources) in API calls.
It dominates plan runtime on large root modules.
Data sources are not refreshed — re-evaluated from scratch.
Drift = a resource changed outside Terraform.
Plan prints `Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform`.
Deleted outside? Refresh marks it gone, plan proposes create.
`terraform refresh` is deprecated since 0.15.4.

blocks.title: `-refresh=false`
blocks.text: Skips every read: much faster, but plans against possibly stale attributes. An emergency flag, not a habit.

items: Backends lock state for the whole write-capable run.
`Error acquiring the state lock` = another run holds it.
Every state write increments the serial.
The plan file records it — that is staleness detection.

blocks.title: force-unlock
items: `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only when certain nothing is applying.
Otherwise you invite concurrent writes and corruption.
`import` blocks (1.5+) are declarative and reviewable.
`plan -generate-config-out=gen.tf` scaffolds the HCL.
`moved` blocks preserve identity across renames.
They survive module extraction with no destroy + create.
Headline first: `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 3 to destroy.`
No-op resources are hidden from the body entirely.
`Changes to Outputs:` is a separate trailing section.
An output-only diff still counts as a change.
`# forces replacement` names the exact triggering field.
`(known after apply)` means the provider computes it later.
One unknown poisons every expression downstream.
An ID inside a template makes the whole string unknown.

blocks.title: (sensitive value)
blocks.text: Masks console output only. The value still exists inside the plan file and the JSON plan.

items: `Objects have changed outside of Terraform` is the drift block.
Listed apart from planned actions — never scroll past it.
`will be replaced, as requested` came from your `-replace`.
Also `is tainted, so must be replaced` and `has been deleted`.
`# module.db.aws_instance.this has moved to ...`
That is `moved` block resolution, zero infrastructure action.
No API calls at all — only a state re-address.
`replace_paths` is the machine form of `# forces replacement`.
Feed `terraform show -json` to OPA or Conftest.
Gate on `delete` against protected resource types.
CI hygiene: `-no-color` and `-compact-warnings`.

blocks.title: Scan Order
items: Search `must be replaced` first.
Then `will be destroyed`.
Then the drift note.
Only then read attribute diffs.
The provider — not core — decides in-place vs replacement.
It signals by returning `RequiresReplace` attribute paths.
SDKv2 sets them with `ForceNew: true`.
Plugin Framework uses `RequiresReplace()` plan modifiers.
Values are `cty` values; unknown is a first-class value.
It propagates through every expression that touches it.
A data source with unknown args is deferred to apply.
Everything it feeds becomes unknown in the plan.

blocks.title: Inconsistent Final Plan
blocks.text: `Provider produced inconsistent final plan` means an applied value differed from a known planned one — a provider bug, not user error.

items: Diffing is whole-object: nested blocks and sets elementwise.
Which is why set ordering changes look like churn.
`ignore_changes` drops attributes from the diff.
`ignore_changes = all` freezes everything after create.
`prevent_destroy` fails any plan proposing destruction.
That includes a `-replace` you asked for yourself.
`precondition` / `postcondition` assert your own invariants.
`check` blocks run after apply and only ever warn.

blocks.title: Blind Spots
items: Provisioners are apply-time only.
They never appear as detail in the plan.
That is one reason they undermine plan review.
The plan file is an internal binary archive.
Plan plus the state snapshot it was based on.
`terraform show -json` is the only stable tooling contract.
Never parse human plan output in CI.
`-target=aws_instance.web` prunes the graph to that node.
Plus everything it depends on, pulled in automatically.
Dependents are excluded — the reverse of most expectations.
Terraform warns every run: resulting state may be incomplete.
Indexed addresses need quoting or the shell eats brackets.
bash: `-target='aws_instance.web[0]'`.
PowerShell: `-target="aws_instance.web[0]"`.
`-target=module.vpc` covers every resource inside it.
Plan-time flag: it cannot be applied to a saved plan file.
Works on `plan`, `apply`, `destroy` and `-refresh-only`.
Provider configuration and variable evaluation still run.
Required variables are still required.

blocks.title: Stale Outputs
blocks.text: Outputs are not fully evaluated in a targeted run, so downstream consumers can read old output values.

items: Routine targeting hides broken configuration.
It produces state no full apply can reproduce.
Always follow with an untargeted `terraform plan`.
Confirm it converges to `No changes.`

lines: terraform plan     # must say: No changes.

blocks.title: Newer Flags
items: `-exclude` is the inverse: everything but these addresses.
Chronic targeting is a structure problem, not a flag problem.
Split the root module so blast radius matches the change.

lines: # destroy then create a healthy resource

items: The modern "turn it off and on again".
Plan-time: the replacement shows in a reviewable plan first.
Repeatable, and combines with `-target` for surgery.
Provider schema decides update vs replace; this is the only override.
`terraform untaint <address>` still clears legacy marks.
Resources taint automatically when creation partially fails.
Also when a creation-time provisioner errors.
The object exists but is not trustworthy.
Builds the new object before removing the old one.
Required for zero-downtime swaps.
It propagates: dependencies needing recreation inherit the flag.
That inheritance is the usual surprising cascade.

blocks.title: Unique Names Break
blocks.text: S3 buckets and IAM roles collide under create_before_destroy — use `name_prefix` or a random suffix.

blocks.title: Deposed Objects
items: An old instance left behind when CBD's destroy step failed.
Shows as `(deposed)` in the plan.
Cleaned up on the next apply.
Blocks replacement too, not only a plain destroy.
Remove the lifecycle block before `-replace` will run.
Guard the data stores you cannot afford to lose.
Dependents referencing computed attributes get their own changes.
Some update, some replace — read the whole plan.
Force downstream re-runs with `terraform_data`.
`triggers_replace` (1.4+) succeeds `null_resource`.

caption.text: Everyone reads the plan output. Almost nobody reads the graph underneath it — which is why `-target` surprises people, why cycles appear out of nowhere, and why a failed apply leaves half a VPC behind. 10 pages on what really happens between plan and apply: the DAG, refresh, every diff symbol, and when `-replace` beats `taint`. Save it for the next 3 a.m. apply.
